item.content:encoded:
There will never be another No. 52 in pinstripes.
On Friday, the Yankees will make official what has felt inevitable for years, retiring CC Sabathia’s number and unveiling a plaque in his honor in Monument Park before New York’s 4:05 p.m. game against the Baltimore Orioles at Yankee Stadium.
It is one of the highest honors the franchise can bestow, and for Sabathia, it comes barely a year after baseball gave him its highest honor.
The big left-hander was inducted into the National Baseball Hall of Fame in 2025, making it to Cooperstown on his first ballot. Now No. 52 will hang permanently at Yankee Stadium, ensuring that the number Sabathia wore for all 11 of his seasons in the Bronx belongs to him forever.
Sabathia will become the 24th Yankees player or manager to have his number retired. Because No. 8 is shared by Bill Dickey and Yogi Berra, 52 will become the 23rd different number removed from circulation by the franchise. He is the first Yankee to receive the honor since Paul O’Neill’s No. 21 was retired in 2022.
A Hall of Fame Career That Found a Home in the Bronx
Sabathia’s road to Monument Park began before he ever put on pinstripes.
He debuted with Cleveland as a 20-year-old in 2001, developed into one of baseball’s premier starting pitchers and won the 2007 American League Cy Young Award. After a remarkable second half with Milwaukee in 2008, when he helped carry the Brewers into the postseason, Sabathia became the centerpiece of the Yankees’ aggressive offseason plans.
New York signed him to a seven-year, $161 million contract in December 2008, at the time the largest free-agent contract ever given to a pitcher.
He immediately delivered.
Sabathia went 19-8 with a 3.37 ERA across 34 starts in 2009, anchoring the rotation as the Yankees returned to the World Series. He was even better when October arrived, earning ALCS MVP honors after going 2-0 with a 1.13 ERA against the Angels. Weeks later, the Yankees were World Series champions for the 27th time.
It would be the beginning of an 11-season relationship between Sabathia and New York.
From 2009 through his retirement in 2019, Sabathia went 134-88 with a 3.81 ERA and 1,700 strikeouts as a Yankee. His name remains scattered throughout the franchise’s pitching record book, ranking fourth in Yankees history in strikeouts, seventh in starts, 10th in wins and 11th in innings pitched.
Sabathia was also a fixture when the games mattered most. In 21 postseason appearances for New York, including 18 starts, he went 8-4 with a 3.42 ERA. At Yankee Stadium, his postseason ERA was just 2.17.
Those numbers tell a large part of the story. They do not tell all of it.
Sabathia became one of the defining personalities of his Yankees era, a clubhouse leader whose importance stretched well beyond what happened every fifth day. By the time he threw the final pitch of his career in 2019, he had long since become synonymous with the pinstripes.
First-Ballot Hall of Famer
Baseball made Sabathia’s place among the game’s greats official in January 2025.
In his first year of eligibility, Sabathia received 86.8 percent of the Baseball Writers’ Association of America vote, easily clearing the 75 percent needed for election into the National Baseball Hall of Fame. He was officially inducted in Cooperstown on July 27, 2025.
His complete career resume left little question about his Cooperstown credentials.
Across 19 Major League seasons with Cleveland, Milwaukee and New York, Sabathia finished 251-161 with a 3.74 ERA. He pitched 3,577 1/3 innings, made six All-Star teams, won a Cy Young Award and struck out 3,093 batters.
He also joined one of baseball’s most exclusive pitching clubs.
Sabathia is one of just 15 pitchers in Major League history to record at least 250 victories and 3,000 strikeouts. When he reached those milestones, only fellow Hall of Famers Randy Johnson and Steve Carlton had done both as left-handers.
And when it came time to decide which team would be represented on his Hall of Fame plaque, Sabathia chose the interlocking NY.
Cooperstown may celebrate his entire career, but Sabathia has made clear where he considers home.
Sabathia’s place in baseball history is already secure, but the family name is still very much part of the game. I had the chance to catch up with him during MLB All-Star Week this summer, just days after the Brewers selected his son, Carsten Sabathia III, in the 2026 MLB Draft. Given CC’s own memorable run in Milwaukee, the connection felt especially fitting, and I asked him if watching his son turn pro had him tempted to pull a LeBron-and-Bronny and come out of retirement for one last chance to share the field.
Another Left-Hander Among Yankees Pitching Royalty
Now Sabathia’s legacy will have a permanent home in center field alongside some of the greatest pitchers to ever wear pinstripes.
When Mariano Rivera received his Monument Park plaque in 2016, he became the ninth Yankees pitcher honored there, joining Lefty Gomez, Whitey Ford, Red Ruffing, Allie Reynolds, Ron Guidry, Goose Gossage, Andy Pettitte and Mel Stottlemyre. Sabathia will add another name to that pitching fraternity.
Several members of that group have an additional distinction that Sabathia will now share.
Ford’s No. 16, Rivera’s No. 42, Pettitte’s No. 46 and Guidry’s No. 49 have all been retired by the Yankees. On Friday, Sabathia’s No. 52 joins them.
There is something especially fitting about Sabathia taking his place alongside Pettitte and Rivera.
They were there with him in 2009, when Sabathia arrived in New York carrying enormous expectations and immediately helped deliver a championship. Derek Jeter’s No. 2, Jorge Posada’s No. 20, Rivera’s No. 42 and Pettitte’s No. 46 have all since been retired. Sabathia now becomes the fifth member of that 2009 championship team to receive the same honor.
Seventeen years after that group brought a World Series trophy back to the Bronx, another piece of the 2009 Yankees will become a permanent part of the ballpark.
52 Forever
Sabathia arrived in New York as an ace with a massive contract and expectations to match.
He leaves his mark on the franchise as something much bigger.
World Series champion. ALCS MVP. Clubhouse leader. More than 1,700 strikeouts in pinstripes. First-ballot Hall of Famer.
And now, forever, No. 52.
Future generations of Yankees fans walking through Monument Park will see Sabathia’s plaque among the franchise’s legends. They’ll look beyond the center-field wall and see his number alongside Ford, Rivera, Pettitte, Guidry and the countless icons who came before him.
Players will come and go. Rotations will change. New aces will take the mound in the Bronx.
But no Yankee will wear 52 again.
That one belongs to CC.

item.content:encoded:
El número 41 apareció en la pantalla del Yankee Stadium y, por un instante, los Yankees volvieron a mirar hacia 1961.
Ben Rice conectó dos cuadrangulares el miércoles ante Tampa Bay para llegar a 41 en la temporada. El segundo puso al primera base de Nueva York en el mismo escalón de jonrones que Pete Alonso, Junior Caminero y Yordan Álvarez en la Liga Americana.
Pero el verdadero alcance de la noche va más allá de una carrera por el liderato de cuadrangulares. Rice acaba de entrar de lleno en la conversación por el MVP de la Liga Americana en la última semana del calendario. Sus números de temporada, después de 162 partidos para Nueva York, son 41 jonrones, 97 carreras anotadas, 148 hits, .263 de promedio, .362 de porcentaje de embasarse y .899 de OPS.
Al otro lado del clubhouse está Cam Schlittler.
El derecho de 25 años se convirtió en el brazo alrededor del cual gira la conversación por el Cy Young de la Americana. Después de 32 apariciones suma 14-6, 1.94 de ERA, 190.2 innings, 234 ponches y 0.91 de WHIP.
Pareja que entraría a los libros de historia de Yankees
Si Rice terminara conquistando el MVP y Schlittler el Cy Young, los Yankees volverían a tener en una misma temporada a los ganadores de los dos premios individuales más importantes de la Liga Americana. La última vez ocurrió en 1961.
Ninguno de los dos llegó a Nueva York con la etiqueta de fenómeno inevitable.
Rice fue elegido por los Yankees en la ronda 12 del Draft de 2021, con la selección 363, procedente de Dartmouth. Schlittler fue seleccionado en la séptima ronda de 2022, con el pick 220, después de jugar en Northeastern.
No fueron elecciones de primera ronda. No fueron nombres destinados desde el Draft a cargar con el uniforme de los Yankees.
Hoy, sin embargo, Rice es un bateador de 41 jonrones y Schlittler es el líder de una rotación que tiene al resto de la industria hablando del Cy Young. MLB describió recientemente la transformación de Schlittler como la de un séptima ronda convertido en All-Star y candidato al premio.
Y mientras Aaron Judge pasó buena parte de 2026 fuera por lesión, Rice terminó ocupando el espacio ofensivo que quedó abierto. Judge apenas disputó 66 encuentros y bateó .241 con 18 cuadrangulares.
¡Qué sucedió en 1961 para los Yankees!
Roger Maris y Whitey Ford escribieron una de las temporadas más reconocibles en la historia de la franquicia.
Maris bateó 61 cuadrangulares, rompió el récord de 60 que Babe Ruth había establecido en 1927 y terminó como MVP de la Liga Americana. En 161 partidos produjo .269/.372/.620, con 141 carreras impulsadas.
Ford, mientras tanto, tuvo una temporada que parecía diseñada para acompañar semejante hazaña: 25-4, 3.21 de ERA, 283 innings y 209 ponches. Ganó el Cy Young.
Los Yankees ganaron 109 juegos, conquistaron la Liga Americana por ocho juegos y después vencieron a Cincinnati en cinco partidos para ganar la Serie Mundial.
Existe además una precisión histórica importante. En 1961 todavía había un solo Cy Young para toda MLB. El premio comenzó a entregarse por separado en cada liga en 1967. Ford fue, por tanto, el ganador absoluto del Cy Young de 1961.
Rice no necesita batear 61 para entrar en esta conversación. Schlittler tampoco necesita reproducir exactamente los números de Ford.
Lo extraordinario sería que dos Yankees seleccionados fuera de las primeras rondas terminaran colocando sus nombres junto a Maris y Ford en la misma fotografía de premios.
¿Hay otros equipos con Cy Young y MVP en la misma temporada?
Antes de 1967, cuando el Cy Young era único para toda MLB, ocurrió con los Braves de 1957 —Hank Aaron y Warren Spahn—, White Sox de 1959 —Nellie Fox y Early Wynn—, Pirates de 1960 —Dick Groat y Vern Law— y Dodgers de 1962 —Maury Wills y Don Drysdale—.
Después de la división del premio por liga, la lista continuó con casos como Boston en 1986, Milwaukee en 1981, Oakland en 1990, Atlanta en 1991, Chicago White Sox en 1993, Oakland en 2002, St. Louis en 2005 y Minnesota en 2006. MLB registra 18 ocasiones en las que dos jugadores de un mismo equipo consiguieron MVP y Cy Young en la misma temporada hasta ese último caso.
También existe otra variante. Un mismo jugador ganó ambos premios en una temporada. Justin Verlander lo hizo en 2011, mientras Clayton Kershaw lo consiguió en 2014. En total, 11 pitchers han ganado Cy Young y MVP en el mismo año.
Por eso el último tramo de 2026 tiene una particularidad para Nueva York.
Today in 1961, Roger Maris of the @Yankees surpasses Babe Ruth’s record with his 61st homerun of the season. ⚾️
(📽 “61” released in 2001)#TodayInSports #PinstripePride

item.content:encoded:
Yankees 6, Angels 3, and for eight and a half innings Wednesday night at Angel Stadium, this one looked like it might stay 1-1 into the parking lot. Cam Schlittler made sure it didn't get out of hand. Austin Wells made sure it never got to an 11th.
Wells' two-out, bases-loaded single in the 10th was the whole game in one swing -- a 1-2 fastball from Luke Murphy that found right field, scoring two and flipping a tossup into a laugher. By the time the inning was over, the Yankees had scored five runs on four straight singles and taken the rubber match of the series, 2-1.
The Turning Point
Extra innings started with Amed Rosario parked on second, the automatic runner, and it took a while to cash him in. José Caballero singled to send him to third. Jazz Chisholm Jr. walked to load the bases. Luis García Jr. popped out for the second out, and for a second it looked like the Yankees might strand the whole mess (they'd left 14 men on base by night's end, which tells you something about how stubborn this offense had been all night).
Then Wells got to Murphy. Two runs scored, Chisholm to third. Cody Bellinger singled him home. Trent Grisham singled Wells home. Ben Rice singled in Bellinger. Four hitters, four singles, five runs, and the Angels never got the third out they needed to escape it.
Star of the Game: Schlittler Rewrites the Record Book
Before any of that happened, Schlittler spent eight innings quietly making history. Two hits. One run. Nine strikeouts. Zero walks. Ninety-nine pitches, 71 of them strikes -- the kind of start where you check the line twice because it doesn't look real for a guy facing a lineup with Mike Trout in it.
That was the 19th time this season Schlittler has allowed a run or fewer in a start. That's a new Yankees single-season record, passing the mark of 18 shared by Ron Guidry's 1978 Cy Young season, Whitey Ford in 1964, and Jack Chesbro all the way back in 1904. Good company. Better yet, Schlittler's still adding to it.
He didn't get the win (no decision, if you're scoring at home), because the Yankees' bats needed extra innings to back him up. He also didn't seem to care. That's usually the sign of the right kind of pitcher.
Detmers Made Him Earn It
Give the Angels' Reid Detmers his due, too. Seven innings, six hits, one earned run, eight strikeouts of his own -- the only damage against him a ground-rule double by Rosario in the fourth that scored Bellinger. For seven innings, this was a legitimate pitchers' duel between two guys who deserved a better final line than "no decision."
Vaughn Grissom's solo homer off Schlittler in the seventh tied it at 1-1 and set up the standoff that lasted until the 10th blew it open.
Boone's Bullpen Math Worked, Barely
David Bednar came in for a scoreless ninth -- one hit, three strikeouts -- and got the win when the Yankees broke through an inning later, which is how it works even if Bednar didn't throw a single pitch in the inning that decided it. Michael Fulmer took the 10th with a five-run lead and made it interesting, giving up a two-run homer to Moisés Ballesteros that scored the Angels' own automatic runner, Wade Meckler. Fulmer got the next two outs anyway. A laugher stayed a win, which is really all that matters in the box score.
Yankees take the series 2-1 after dropping the opener 1-10 on Monday, and they move to 80-60, three and a half back of the Rays with a month to play. San Diego's up next.
Jimmy writes the Bronx Pinstripes game recap after every Yankees game. Beat-reporter pacing, fan's heartbeat. He calls opposing players by last name and has no patience for dead-air innings.

item.content:encoded:
Cards
Crisp design, colorful action photos and star players make 1956 Topps Baseball a popular vintage set for collectors
The 1956 Topps set is arguably one of the most aesthetically pleasing baseball card sets of all time.
A crisp design, full-color artwork featuring dual action and profile shots, clean white borders and all the best players in the game make the set truly iconic.
It is instantly recognizable to any vintage baseball card buff.
Related Content:
Add in the fact that over half the players come in white and gray back variations—some cards rarer than others—and every card is widely available 70 years after production, the set’s lasting impact on the hobby is no surprise.
“I think you’re not going to get a lot of pushback from a lot of collectors that know that era. It would be hard to battle that set, because it’s got everything,” said Mike Baker, founder of Mike Baker Authenticated.
New York Yankees great Mickey Mantle is the crown jewel of the 340-card set. But there isn’t a lack of star power.
“It’s one of those weird sets from the ’50s that even though there’s a Luis Aparicio rookie, it’s really not anchored by that,” said Leighton Sheldon, owner of Vintage Breaks and Just Collect. “It’s anchored by the fact there’s just every available star of the day: Ted Williams, Jackie Robinson, Al Kaline, Willie Mays. The list just goes on and on. And those cards are highly coveted because of the design, because it shows a few different aspects of the player.”
Former Heritage Auctions Executive Vice President of Sports Joe Orlando agrees. The 1956 set features second-year cards of Sandy Koufax, Roberto Clemente and Harmon Killebrew and early cards of Mantle, Mays and Hank Aaron.
“The star combination across the board is so terrific,” Orlando said. “If you were to ask what’s the one relatively weak spot of this set, it doesn’t have as strong of a rookie card class as some of the sets around it. In 1955, you have one of the all-time great rookie card selections in Koufax, Clemente and Killebrew. In 1957, a year later, you have Don Drysdale, Frank Robinson, Brooks Robinson, it just keeps going with great rookie cards in that set. But in ’56 you have Luis Aparicio, a Hall of Fame shortstop, great player, but that’s basically the extent of the major names.”
MANTLE RETURNS
One main reason the set is so special and adored by collectors is it featured the reintroduction of Mantle back into Topps. The slugger was included in Topps’ 1952 and ’53 sets, but rival card company Bowman inked Mantle to an exclusive contract. He was noticeably excluded from Topps’ 1954 and ’55 releases. However, after Topps bought out its only competitor in January 1956, Mantle, Yankees pitcher Whitey Ford and Cleveland Indians pitcher Bob Feller all made their way back to Topps.
“Having Mantle back in Topps was such a huge moment for the company, because Mickey Mantle was the most popular player in baseball,” Orlando said. “Having him back in the set is a huge, huge part of its appeal. And, of course, in 1956 he just happens to reach the Triple Crown, which is like the stars aligned for Mantle that year.”
The ’56 Mantle is his only horizontal card during his illustrious Topps run. Mantle’s first ever Topps card in 1952 always receives accolades as one of the most iconic cards in the hobby. But his ’56 card is right up there with the ’53 release as being in the top three of Mantle’s most coveted cards.
“If you look at the card, it’s such a great looking card,” Orlando said. “He’s smiling ear to ear on his portrait side of the picture, there’s a beautiful action shot of him going into the stands, making a leaping grab in the background. Sometimes the design comes together in a way that just creates such a visually appealing card, and in this case, I think that’s a huge part of it. It’s just such a great looking card of Mantle, coupled with the other attributes that it’s absolutely one of his most popular issues.”
Having Mantle back in its product was monumental for Topps. And the company, in just its sixth year of making cards, took full advantage of having the face of America’s Pastime in its set.
After a successful year with the 1955 set, which featured a very similar look the following year, Topps upped its print run in ’56. That is evident in PSA’s Population Report from that year.
As of the end of January 2026, PSA had graded 212,795 cards from the 1955 set. The number of slabs jumped to 391,296—nearly double—for the 1956 set.
Having so much product around even 70 years after its release is advantageous for set collectors. The ’56 set can be achieved in high grades since there are so many prime examples.
“In 1956, because it is more attainable than 1955 or 1954, it actually invites more participation, more competition because there’s more product out there,” said Orlando, who used to be the president of PSA. “So, while it isn’t the toughest of the ’50s Topps sets, because the design is so appealing and the star selection is also so appealing and the cards are attainable in high grade, it actually makes for a nice combination and an inviting one for a lot of collectors.”
Collectors seemed to have taken care of their ’56 Topps cards, even seven decades ago. Remarkably, there are just shy of 80,000 copies that have received PSA 8 grades or higher. There are 305 cards that have reached Gem Mint PSA 10 status.
“The fact that they’ve got white borders, too, generally those cards are going to grade a tad bit better,” longtime baseball card collector Ryan Hoge said. “If you look at the population, there’s a heavy concentration of grades between 6 and 8, which is good for vintage. If you fast forward to say I want to look at like ’71 as a counterpoint, black borders, your percentage of 8s and 9s is infinitely smaller, if you look at the overall split across the PSA grades.”
Hoge, who is President of Grading at Collectors, the parent company of PSA, SGC and Beckett, noted that 1956 Topps baseball is one of the most popular vintage sets for passionate collectors who use the PSA Registry.
Hoge personally loves the ’56 release. He doesn’t collect the set, but he considers four 1956 cards he owns among the favorites in his collection. Hoge has a Mantle PSA 8.5 and Robinson, Mays and Aaron cards all slabbed in PSA 8.
“These are some of the coolest cards in my collection, the Mantle in particular is awesome. It was his Triple Crown year,” Hoge said. “I think the innovation with the profile shot and the action shot just adds to the eye appeal on the front of the card. Then on the back it has the information, the storytelling; the backs of these cards had all sorts of fun trivia type nuggets about the players and then their stats. Just awesome stuff.”
For how accessible single cards—raw and graded—and sets are from 1956, sealed wax and even wrappers are impossible to find, noted Sheldon. Over the years, there haven’t been any major finds unearthing a large offering of unripped packs.
SET COLLECTORS UNITE
A longtime set collector whose name is plastered all over the PSA Set Registry, John Evanoff has finished off Topps baseball set runs from 1952-67 and 1969-72.
It has been Evanoff’s goal to have every set he completes rank in the top 10 on PSA’s registry. In order to achieve that, all the cards need to be in high grades, 8s and up.
“It became a challenge,” Evanoff said. “That registry is addictive.”
Since he was on the verge of retirement, to financially afford to complete the high-graded sets, he needed to sell off some of his cards. One of the five sets he held onto was 1956 Topps.
Evanoff initially pieced together the ’56 set in just five months in fall 2015.
“It’s an easy set to finish in high grade, 8 or up, if you’ve got the money,” Evanoff said. “But back then they weren’t all that expensive. For example, I got the Mantle in an 8.5 for $5,700 at the 2015 National.”
Evanoff also acquired a number of the big stars in the set from Memory Lane Inc. He picked up Robinson and Aaron in PSA 8.5 for $2,000 apiece. Now those examples sell in the five-figure range.
Once Evanoff knocked off some of the most expensive cards, his new goal was to crack the top five in the PSA Set Registry.
“Which means, now you’ve got to go for 9s,” Evanoff said. “Now, look at the price of those cards; they’re crazy expensive.”
Evanoff—who has the No. 3-ranked Current Finest set in the PSA Set Registry for 1956 Topps—is constantly upgrading his cards. He owns 236 cards graded a PSA 9, 29 in PSA 8.5 and 77 in PSA 8.
Evanoff has invested a great deal of time and money into his ’56 set. He recently spent $29,000 on a PSA 9 of Roy Campanella. The toughest 9 for Evanoff to track down has been of Red Schoendienst. There are 17 Gray backs in a 9, but Evanoff has been chasing that grade for six years to no avail.
Evanoff makes it a point to meet up with 1956 Topps set collectors at the National Sports Collectors Convention. He planned to sell a PSA 8 at the show when he upgrades to a 9. Evanoff also sells a lot on the Facebook group for 1956 Topps set collectors.
“It’s a competition,” said Evanoff, whose set is GPA weighted at 8.78. “I love it. That’s why I do it.”
For set collector Lanny Ribes, the 1956 set has really grown on him over the years. He’s a huge fan of the ’55 release but the ’56 set wasn’t his favorite for quite some time.
Ribes’ son, Anthony, plays college baseball at the University of Illinois Springfield. Ribes uses different Topps card designs from over the years to make cards of his son.
“Whenever I design a different one, I fall in love with it just because of the colors and the fonts and everything else,” Ribes said. “So, ’56 for me it was pretty much exactly like 1955, except it had that action photo in the background. I thought that was cool.
“That was like the first action photos. I know it’s artwork, but the first action on a card you could really see. The Mickey Mantle and the Hank Aaron making plays over the wall and sliding plays at home plate. So, for me it was a combination of the artwork is absolutely gorgeous, the colors really pop and you’ve got that action part on every card—it was the first of its kind.”
WHITE VS GRAY
One aspect that separates the 1956 set from other vintage sets is it was the final year Topps produced larger cards. The dimensions were 2 5/8-by- 3 3/4. The following year Topps transitioned to 2½-by-3½, which is the size that has been used ever since.
Topps also experimented with different backs for its cards. Cards numbered #1-180 have cardboard backs with both white and gray. For numbers #1-100, the white backs are more common; for numbers #101-180, the gray backs are more common.
For example, Ted Williams’ card #5 has a PSA population of 5,319 for white backs and 2,344 for gray backs. Mantle’s card #135, on the other hand, has been graded 10,334 times in a gray back and just 1,109 in a white back.
The rarer cards certainly demand a higher premium. A Mantle white back in a PSA 5 sold in October 2025 for $4,500. A Mantle in a gray in the same grade went for $2,800 in January 2026.
“Having the gray back and the white back varieties is definitely a challenge,” Baker said. “The white backs are incredibly more challenging than their gray back counterparts—the population report shows that. But I think it adds another little flare to it. Having as many varieties in that set is kind of fun.”
The ’56 set has stood the test of time with collectors 70 years after its release. The great designs and star players keep the set extremely popular.
“Certainly, I mean no disrespect in saying this, but I’ve heard this expression that a ’56 Topps set is a poor man’s ’52,” Sheldon said. “The reason being is you had the stars of the day, but there’s no high numbers. In other words, you don’t have to buy a random common that costs you hundreds of dollars in VG, even like a ’52 Topps, because there’s no high-number series. So, for collectors on a budget, still being able to access a Jackie Robinson or Mickey Mantle that are not high numbers that are beautiful cards, you have to pay a fraction of what the ’52s go for.”

For a historic franchise like the New York Yankees, rotation stability is paramount over the long haul of a 162-game season. That makes Cam Schlittler’s dominant breakout campaign all the more remarkable—so much so that manager Aaron Boone believes the young right-hander has built a compelling case to take home the American League Cy Young Award.
When asked about Schlittler’s transformative presence in the rotation, Boone didn’t mince words: “Well, he’s gonna win the Cy Young!” The manager’s ringing endorsement underscores just how dominant Schlittler has been on the mound this year.
While Boone continues to navigate rotation depth with Ryan Weathers sidelined for the remainder of the regular season, Schlittler gives the Yankees a legitimate ace to rely on as they gear up for October.
On the offensive side, Boone is also monitoring the return timeline for slugger Aaron Judge, who was sidelined with a calf strain. In the meantime, the Yankees skipper has relied on depth options like Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger to keep the lineup producing.
Key milestones driving Schlittler’s Cy Young case
A stellar 2026 breakout campaign with the Yankees has vaulted Schlittler directly into the front-runner conversation for the American League Cy Young Award. Stepping up as the de facto ace while Gerrit Cole missed time, Schlittler has delivered elite run suppression, swing-and-miss stuff, and exceptional durability.
Here is a breakdown of the key numbers and milestones anchoring Schlittler’s Cy Young candidacy:
- 1.95 ERA: Schlittler took over the MLB ERA lead in September, standing as the only qualified starter with an ERA under 2.00.
- Historical run: His 1.71 ERA through his first 16 starts marked the lowest ERA by a Yankees starter through that stretch since Hall of Famer Whitey Ford in 1964.
- 228 Strikeouts in 184.2 IP (11.1 K/9): Schlittler eclipsed the 200-strikeout mark on August 28 against Boston, becoming the fourth-youngest pitcher in franchise history to achieve the feat.
- Signature outings: Highlighted by a career-high 13-strikeout performance against the Cincinnati Reds on June 19, along with double-digit strikeout shutouts against Philadelphia (12 K) and Atlanta (11 K).
Other top Cy Young contenders
Schlittler isn’t running unopposed in a tightly contested American League race. Strong campaigns from power arm Dylan Cease of the Toronto Blue Jays and left-hander Garrett Crochet of the Boston Red Sox keep them firmly in the mix.
Over in the National League, the Cy Young field features plenty of heavy hitters, headlined by Milwaukee Brewers phenom Jacob Misiorowski, Atlanta Braves veteran Chris Sale, and the Philadelphia Phillies duo of Cristopher Sanchez and Jesus Luzardo.

item.content:encoded:
Even the biggest of homers couldn’t predict just how dominant Cam Schlittler would be this season. The ace of the New York Yankees has cemented himself as one of the top pitchers in all of baseball and proven that last year was not a fluke. Schlittler’s 2026 season may even go down as one of the best pitching performances in the entire history of the franchise. Despite the Yankees’ storied franchise, only six pitchers have won the Cy Young award for the team. Schlittler is likely about to change that.
With 6.0 fWAR accumulated throughout the 2026 season, Schlittler is tied with Milwaukee Brewers’ sensation Jacob Misiorowski for the league lead among pitchers. It’s no coincidence that both hurlers are the favorites to take home the Cy Young in their respective leagues. For Schlittler, he’d not only be the seventh Yankees pitcher to win the award, but he’d also be the youngest.
As the Yankees prepare for another postseason run, they will hope that Schlittler’s historic performance is able to carry over into October. As history has taught us, the Yankees win when their pitchers win.
Yankees Complete History of Cy Young Award Winners
It’s hard to fathom that the Yankees only average a Cy Young award winner every 20 years or so. From Mike Mussina to CC Sabathia, the franchise has certainly featured plenty of Hall of Fame pitchers that have come close to winning the award. Mussina was overshadowed by teammate Roger Clemens during his stellar 2001 campaign with the Yankees. Sabathia got as close to third place in the voting following his 2010 season.
Even the great Mariano Rivera couldn’t quite do enough to sway the voters and win the elusive award as a reliever. He finished in the top three of voting four separate times. This includes two seasons when he finished in the top 10 of the MVP race. It’s rare, but pitchers have occasionally made strong cases for MVP.
We’ll detail the six previous Yankees who actually managed to cross the finish line and why they deserved to take home the top pitching award. And because a Yankees season isn’t complete without a World Series title, we’ll also note how far a Cy Young winner got the team in the postseason.
Gerrit Cole, 2023
As the most recent Yankees pitcher to win the award, Gerrit Cole did something in 2023 that only one other player had accomplished in the team’s history, winning the award by unanimous decision. With all 30 first place votes, Cole more than doubled the amount of points that second-place pitcher Sonny Gray received.
As you might imagine, Cole’s 2023 is his most impressive season with the Yankees since joining the club in 2020. He struck out 222 hitters across 209 innings pitched. Although his 3.16 FIP doesn’t scream “elite pitcher,” he allowed just 157 hits while surrendering just 48 walks.
Despite Cole’s brilliance, the club finished with a mediocre 82-80 record, missing out on the playoffs for the first time since the 2016 season, though you couldn’t blame Cole for that. He boasted a 1.03 ERA and a minuscule 0.686 WHIP over his last five starts of the season, including a two-hit shutdown against the Toronto Blue Jays in his last start of the season. If only Aaron Judge hadn't run toe-first into the wall at Dodger Stadium.
Roger Clemens, 2001
As mentioned earlier, Clemens scooped away a lot of votes from Mussina when he won the Cy Young in 2001. Some would argue that Clemens probably stole that award, but you can’t deny that he still had a very good season.
With more emphasis placed on individual wins back then, Clemens boasted 20 wins to go alongside his 213 strikeouts. Clemens’ 2001 season would probably be considered his weakest of his seven award-winning seasons. But hey, it was the early 2000s. People voted more on vibes than actual performance.
Clemens’ 3.29 FIP that season was enough to help take the Yankees to the World Series, where they lost in heartbreaking fashion to the Arizona Diamondbacks. But we don’t have to dwell on that part.
Ron Guidry, 1978
Before Clemens won the award in 2001, it had been 23 years since a Yankees pitcher won it. But oh man, did Ron Guidry ever earn the award in 1978. With a 1.74 ERA across 273 1/3 innings pitched, his season is what many consider to be the best by a pitcher in team history. His home run per nine rate of 0.4 is almost laughable.
Even by modern metrics, Guidry was the clear-cut winner that season. His 2.19 FIP and 208 ERA+ was leaps and bounds better than any other pitcher up for consideration that year, which is why he became the first Yankees pitcher to win the award unanimously.
Guidry was a large reason that the team won 100 games that year. The Yankees would carry that tremendous momentum into the postseason and defeat the Los Angeles Dodgers in the World Series.
Sparky Lyle, 1977
Unlike the long wait in between Clemens and Guidry winning the Cy Young, the Yankees actually had quite the time in the late 70s when it came to award-winning pitchers. Before Guidry, the team saw reliever Sparky Lyle take home the award in 1977. He became just the second reliever in MLB history to win the honor. Since then, seven more relievers have joined the rare club.
When looking at his numbers, you probably wouldn’t really consider Lyle to be a dominant force out of the bullpen. Despite that, he was certainly one of the most effective pitchers in the league. With just 68 strikeouts in 137 innings, Lyle didn’t just rely on swing and misses to get outs. He collected 13 wins and 26 saves, demonstrating just how pivotal he was to the Yankees.
With Lyle coming out of the pen, the Yankees won 100 games in the regular season. He then helped pave the way to a World Series title over the Dodgers.
Whitey Ford, 1961
With 236 career wins and six World Series rings in his collection, Whitey Ford is one of the foremost Yankees winners in team history. In 1961, he added a Cy Young to his trophy case. At 32 years old, he threw a career-high 283 innings, which included 11 complete games and three shutouts.
Ford’s 1961 season may be outshined in the annals of history by Roger Maris’ record-setting performance, but that doesn’t make it any less impressive. Like other pitchers on this list, Ford didn’t put up mind-boggling numbers or boast off-the-charts metrics. Outside of innings pitched, he didn’t really do one thing extremely well. However, he did do just about everything very well.
Ford was more than enough of a pitcher to be considered the ace of a team that some argue to be one of the best teams in MLB history. With 109 wins and a World Series title, it is hard to argue against that claim.
Bob Turley, 1958
Just three years before Ford won his Cy Young, Bob Turley became the first Yankees pitcher to win the award in 1958. Once again, like a number of other Yankees on this list, Turley’s 1958 season isn’t something that you would circle as an all-time great year. His 4.04 WHIP and 119 ERA+ were shockingly poor in hindsight.
Turley probably became the first Yankees pitcher to steal the award from a more deserving pitcher as well. Sorry, Warren Spahn. While Turley threw 245 1/3 innings, including 19 complete games, he was an especially wild pitcher. Turley walked 128 batters, nearly double the amount of walks surrendered by the second and third place pitchers in the Cy Young voting combined that year.
With all of that said, Turley pitched well enough to help lead the Yankees to 92 wins. They then went on to defeat the Milwaukee Braves in seven games in the World Series. When all is said and done, what more could you ask for?
